A monist is a person who believes that all of reality — everything that has ever existed or could exist — ultimately comes down to one single, fundamental type of thing. That's the whole idea. A monist looks at the universe and says: "Strip everything back far enough, and you'll find that it's all made of, or reducible to, one underlying thing."

This might sound simple, but it is a profound philosophical position, and what that "one thing" actually is is where monists begin to disagree with each other.
Why This Is a Big Deal

To appreciate what a monist is, consider a question that has puzzled humans for thousands of years: What is the world made of, at the deepest level?

Your body, your thoughts, a rock, a sound, an emotion, the laws of mathematics — are these all totally different categories of existence? Or does some single, unifying principle connect and underlie all of them?

A monist says: yes, there is one underlying unity. A monist rejects the idea that reality is fundamentally divided into separate, irreducible categories.

Because monists agree on "one thing" but disagree on what that one thing is, there are several distinct varieties:

The Materialist Monist (also called a Physicalist Monist) believes that everything is, at bottom, physical matter or physical energy. Your thoughts, your feelings, your consciousness — a materialist monist says these are not a separate, mysterious kind of stuff; they are just the brain doing physical things. Science, in many ways, leans toward this view. If you believe the mind is just the brain, and the brain is just matter, you are thinking like a materialist monist.

The Idealist Monist takes the exact opposite position. They believe the one fundamental thing is mind or consciousness, not matter. Physical objects, they argue, only exist as perceptions or ideas within a mind. The world is not a collection of solid objects — it is, at its root, mental. The philosopher George Berkeley held this view. He argued that to exist is to be perceived — if you cannot perceive something, it has no independent existence.

The Neutral Monist refuses to pick a side between mind and matter. They say the one fundamental substance is neither mental nor physical — it is something neutral, and both mind and matter are just different expressions of it, the way steam and ice are both expressions of the same underlying thing (water). The philosopher William James and, at certain points, Bertrand Russell leaned toward this view.

The Priority Monist takes a more modern and subtle approach. They do not necessarily say everything is made of the same stuff, but they argue there is one fundamental whole — the universe itself — and everything else (every particle, every object, every person) is a derivative part of that whole, not a standalone thing. The parts depend on the whole for their existence, not the other way around. Think of it like this: you might say a wave is "part of the ocean," but the wave has no real existence on its own — it is the ocean doing something. Priority monism, associated with philosopher Jonathan Schaffer, extends this logic to everything.

The philosopher most associated with monism is Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677). He argued that there is only one substance in the universe, and he identified it as God, or Nature (he used both terms interchangeably, treating them as the same thing). Everything — your mind, your body, a tree, a star — is just a different expression or "mode" of this single substance. There is no God separate from the universe, and there is no universe separate from God. They are one and the same thing, seen from different angles. This view is also called pantheism (the idea that God and the universe are identical), and Spinoza is its most celebrated defender.

Understanding what a monist opposes sharpens the definition considerably.

A monist is the opposite of a dualist. A dualist believes reality has two fundamental, irreducible types of things. The most famous dualist is René Descartes, who argued that the universe contains both mind (a non-physical, thinking substance) and matter (a physical, extended substance) — and these two are genuinely separate and different in nature. The classic "mind-body problem" — how does the non-physical mind control the physical body? — arises directly from dualism. A monist dissolves this problem by refusing to accept the division in the first place.

A monist is also different from a pluralist, who believes there are many different fundamental types of things or substances, not just one or two.

So the spectrum runs: monism (one) → dualism (two) → pluralism (many).

The word "monist" is most at home in philosophy, but the concept appears in other fields too.

In religion and spirituality, a monist is someone who believes that all of existence — the divine, the human, the natural world — is ultimately one unified reality. This is a central idea in certain schools of Hindu thought, particularly Advaita Vedanta, which teaches that the individual self (Atman) and the ultimate reality (Brahman) are not two different things but one and the same. Many forms of mysticism across different traditions carry this monist flavour.

In law and political theory, a monist is someone who believes that international law and a nation's domestic law are not two separate legal systems but form a single, unified legal order. In this view, when a country signs an international treaty, that law automatically becomes part of the country's own law without needing to be separately passed as domestic legislation. This stands in contrast to a dualist legal position, which holds that international and domestic law are entirely separate systems that must be deliberately "translated" from one to the other.
If you ever need to recall this word in an instant: a monist is someone who believes that, when you get to the very bottom of things, everything is one.
